routes.label: Center distances and a right triangle

question:
Circle \(C_1\) and \(C_2\) each have radius \(1,\) and the distance between their centers is \(\frac{1}{2}.\) Circle \(C_3\) is the largest circle internally tangent to both \(C_1\) and \(C_2.\) Circle \(C_4\) is internally tangent to both \(C_1\) and \(C_2\) and externally tangent to \(C_3.\) What is the radius of \(C_4?\)

[Figure 1](figures/2023_AMC_10A_Q22_question_fig1.svg)
solution:
Joining the centers turns tangency into length equations: internal tangency gives the difference of the radii, while external tangency gives their sum.

Let \(O_1,O_2\) be the centers of the unit circles and \(M\) their midpoint, so \(O_1M=O_2M=1/4\). Any circle of radius \(t\), where \(0<t<1\), lying inside and internally tangent to both unit circles has a center \(P\) satisfying
\[
O_1P=O_2P=1-t.
\]
Thus \(P\) lies on the perpendicular bisector of \(O_1O_2\). The Pythagorean theorem gives
\[
(1-t)^2=\frac{1}{16}+MP^2,
\]
with the same equality holding directly when \(P=M\). Since \(1-t>0\), we obtain \(1-t\ge 1/4\), or \(t\le 3/4\). A circle centered at \(M\) with radius \(3/4\) attains this bound: its center distance plus its radius is \(1/4+3/4=1\) for each unit circle. Therefore \(C_3\) has center \(M\) and radius \(3/4\).

Now let \(Q\) be the center of \(C_4\) and \(r\) its radius. Internal tangency again gives \(O_1Q=O_2Q=1-r\), so \(Q\) lies on the same perpendicular bisector. External tangency to \(C_3\) gives \(MQ=3/4+r\). Consequently, the right triangle \(O_1MQ\) satisfies
\[
\frac{1}{16}+\left(\frac34+r\right)^2=(1-r)^2.
\]
Expanding cancels the \(r^2\) terms, leaving
\[
\frac58+\frac32r=1-2r,
\qquad
\frac72r=\frac38.
\]
Hence \(r=3/28\). This radius is positive and less than \(1\); placing \(Q\) on either side of \(M\) at distance \(6/7\) gives \(O_1Q=O_2Q=25/28=1-r\), so all three tangencies hold. The radius is therefore \(\boxed{\frac{3}{28}}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{D}}\).
